image_description:
1. **Chart type**: Scatter plot with colored group regions/contours and a few text annotations.

2. **Layout techniques**:  
- Single-panel chart  
- No faceting or small multiples  
- No stacking  
- Uses color-coded category overlays (semi-transparent regions) to show clusters/ranges for vehicle types

3. **Data variables**

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Average cost per month | Quantitative | Position on x-axis |
| Average carbon dioxide emissions per mile | Quantitative | Position on y-axis |
| Vehicle powertrain/type (Traditional gas-powered cars, Hybrid and plug-in hybrid vehicles, Electric cars, Diesel cars, Fuel cell) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue of points and shaded regions; text labels for groups |
| Individual vehicle/model | Categorical/nominal | Individual point marks; text annotations for selected models (e.g., Honda Civic, Nissan Leaf, Toyota Sequoia, Lexus GX) |

comments.raw_comment:
What do I notice?
- High end SUVS such as the Toyota Sequoia and the Lexus GX are at the top of carbon dioxide emissions and price.
- All fully electric cars have less carbon emissions than gas-powered cars and diesel cars with an average of about 200 grams per mile.
- Hybrid and diesel cars are in the middle for both price and carbon emissions.
- There really is no reason not to choose electric cars other than preference since the price on average is lower than most other types of cars, and the emissions are so low.

What do I wonder?
- I wonder why the hybrid cars still do get emissions higher than some gas-powered.
- I wonder why people still don't choose electric cars even with the low price average and low carbon emissions.

What impact does this have on you and your community?
This graph impacts me and my community because it shows how electric vehicles can be cheap and save the environment, while showing how the other types are over all more expensive for the consumer, and for the environment.

What’s going on in this graph? Write a catchy headline that captures the graph’s main idea.
This graph shows that over all, EV's are cheaper in price over time, and helps the environment more than other types of cars. A good headline for this graph would be "EV's: The cars that save the environment and your wallet!"

I noticed that electric cars have a substantially lower average carbon dioxide emission than most of the other cars listed on the graph. These electric cars also cost less than many other cars. I also noticed that the carbon dioxide emissions of the hybrid cars can vary widely. Some of the hybrid cars produce less carbon dioxide than the other vehicles, but many of hybrid cars emit more carbon dioxide than the gas-powered cars. The gas-powered cars have the largest range in carbon dioxide emissions and average cost of maintenance. The diesel cars are very concentrated in the average cost per month and the amount of emitted carbon dioxide, both of which being very high. 

These observations cause me to wonder why vehicles that are more costly and worse for the environment are used. If more average civilians can use electric cars, or gas-powered cars with lower carbon dioxide emission rates, it could help to slow climate change and save money. I also wonder how we can help implement a change to persuade people to use more cost effective cars that produce less carbon dioxide. 

The impact the information in this graph has on me and my community is the amount of carbon dioxide produced by different types of cars and subsequent climate change. If more vehicles continue using fossil fuels, the effects of climate change will have a serious impact. Conversely, if more people use electric cars, it can lower carbon emissions from vehicles considerably, which would be beneficial.

Traditional gas-powered cars have both the greatest carbon dioxide emissions and the highest average costs per month. There is a group of diesel cars that sit rather in the middle of the graph with higher average costs per month but not the highest and high carbon dioxide emission but not the greatest.
I wonder what a fuel cell is. I also wonder how many people drive diesel cars compared to electric cars and gas-powered cars. What factors do people consider buying their car? Do they care more about the usage of the car, whether it's eco-friendly, or the price? I wonder what aspects of electric cars are allow them to have such low average costs per month.

This impacts the community because carbon dioxide emissions contribute to pollution and global warming. What do you notice?
I notice that electric cars generally cost the least amount of money per month while also creating the least average carbon emissions per mile. Additionally, traditional gas powered cars create the most amount of carbon emissions per mile, but can range in price from most expensive to least expensive per month. This is likely because traditional gas-powered cars are the most abundantly distributed car. Hybrid cars are an average of traditional gas-powered cars and electric cars. They emit less carbon dioxide per mile than gas-powered cars, but the emit more carbon dioxide per mile than electric cars. 

What do you wonder?
From what I have heard from my peers, people refrain from thinking about buying electric cars because they believe they are too expensive. If people knew about the cost efficiency of electric cars, would they be more willing to buy them? 

What impact does this have on you and your community?
The current climate crisis will ultimately effect almost every person in my generation. Many scientists believe that air pollution has caused an increase in cancers, cognitive decline, and depression. Carbon emissions are one of the most significant causes of this air pollution. Thus, the information in this graph should be used to motivate people to buy electric cars instead of traditional gas-powered cars.

comments.raw_comment: Based on the data presented in the graph, our group found that there are five main groups of vehicles presented, consisting of traditional gas-powered cars, diesel cars, hybrid vehicles, fuel cell, and electric cars. Furthermore, we noticed gas-powered cars have the highest emissions rate while also maintaining a high average cost. Electric cars, on the other hand, had mostly similar monthly costs as their gas-powered counterparts but had far fewer emissions per mile. Based on these observations, we wondered what if the size of a car had any correlation to CO2 emission levels as well as if the dots that are clustered together have the same manufacturer? Lastly, our group analyzed the impact that the data presented in this graph had on us and our community. In today’s environment where pollution is a major topic, this graph helped reveal what cars are not only environmentally friendly, but also helped save consumer’s money. Our headline for this graph would be, “Average Cost per Month vs. Average CO2 Emissions for Different Fuel Using Cars.”

comments.raw_comment:
My team noticed that gas cars are more expensive than electric cars (which was contrary to what most of us had naturally assumed). We also noticed that there’s an outlying piece of data with the intriguing name of a fuel cell car. 
After looking upon this beautiful graph, my team and I had a few questions pop into our minds, such as: Do you think the number of fuel cars will increase in coming years? And if so, by how much? Why are there so few fuel cell cars? Are they really expensive to make? Why do gas cars have such a wide range of CO2 emissions?
We also had a few questions on how this might impact our community: Will charging stations be popping up around the community for the convenience of electric car owners? Will electric cars become more common?
As a final task, our group was asked to create a catchy headline that could capture the attention of such a grand audience as those who read The New York Times. Personally, I love to be dramatic, and as the scribe of our group I have full reign over adding whatever amount of soap opera I want to the headline, so in the end, our two possible titles turned out to be something like this:  “The Cost of Humanities Future” and “Carbon Boom or Bust”

comments.raw_comment: Based on the graph, we noticed that electric cars emit less Carbon Dioxide and cost less to maintain every month. This can be shown through the Toyota Sequoia and the Nissan leaf, the prior of which has one of the highest costs of maintenance and high Carbon Dioxide emissions. The Nissan Leaf, on the other hand, is an electric car that emits little Carbon Dioxide and is one of the least expensive cars to maintain. Based on the information and our brainstorming, we wondered if there is a correlation between maintenance costs per month and carbon dioxide emissions. Many cars that emit less carbon dioxide also cost less to maintain, this is true for many electric, hybrid, and gas-powered cars. The traditional gas-powered cars that emit more carbon dioxide have a great impact on our community because climate change is hurting our environment every day. It has become a more and more pressing issue with each passing day. Being able to be conscious of the different emissions caused by these different cars, and how they are going to affect your wallet will seriously impact our purchasing habits and the environment. Our catchy headline that captures the graphs’ main idea is “Save Your Wallet And The Planet.”

The graph appeared in The New York Times.  Which cars reduce the true costs of our car-buying decisions – both for the planet and our budgets?

By Friday morning, we’ll reveal on the “What’s Going On In This Graph?” website, the link to the article that included this graph and much more.  

Note that you can get a link to your response to share with your teacher and classmates by clicking the response box below your response “Email me when my comment is published.”  

Please visit our archive to see all graphs in this series (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphs).

The electric cars of course have the lowest carbon emissions while the gas-powered cars have the highest. The Nissan Leaf seems to be one of the cheapest and low-emission vehicles on the graph. I wonder if the vehicles on the top right of the graph are larger (SUVs, vans, etc). I also wonder what the difference between diesel and gas-powered cars is.
My community is heavily sprawled and there is not much public transportation, so cars are a necessity for most people. This graph would be very helpful for people in my community who are looking to buy a car that is environmentally friendly yet affordable. Unfortunately, even electric cars have carbon emissions. Hopefully in the future, cars can become a thing of the past as our society finds more environmentally friendly ways of life. Designing cities and neighborhoods which are pedestrian friendly and not as sprawled is definitely a step in the right direction.
